analysis.one_liner: Bars giant online platforms from promoting their own products and from selling web hosting to others.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a cosponsor, or a vote in the two years it sat in the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the largest online platforms — those with over $1.5 billion in global revenue and tens of millions of users — to stop selling and promoting their own products on their own sites, and to sell off any company they own that sells there. It also would have barred them from selling web hosting or internet infrastructure services like content delivery and cyberattack protection to anyone else, and given the FTC, state attorneys general, and private plaintiffs the power to enforce those rules. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary consumers and the small businesses that sell through Amazon, Google Shopping, and similar platforms would have gained. The bill would have stopped a platform from steering shoppers to its own cheaper-to-make products over outside sellers' goods, which is a classic way dominant platforms squeeze rivals. [S2][S3] Users of websites and online services would have gained from conflict-of-interest rules separating the companies that run platforms from the companies that provide the hosting, security, and backbone infrastructure those platforms run on. [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and small sellers on big platforms

how_it_helps.text: Bars a covered platform from selling, advertising, or promoting its own goods and services on its own site, ending the practice of a platform steering users to its own products over outside sellers'.

Requires any affiliation, common ownership, or control of an entity that sells on the platform to be terminated or liquidated within one year, and bans future acquisitions of such entities — a structural separation rather than just a conduct rule.

Enforces the rules three ways: the FTC would hire staff and run annual audits of each covered platform, state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents, and any injured person could sue for up to $1,000,000 per violation.

analysis.who_pays: The giant platforms themselves — Amazon, Google, and any company over the bill's size thresholds — would bear the cost. They would have to stop selling their own products on their own sites, spin off or sell any company that sells on their platforms, and get out of the business of hosting other companies' websites, shedding revenue streams worth tens of billions of dollars and restructuring their companies within one year. [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Amazon, Google, and other giant platforms

drawbacks.text: The hosting ban is a blunt instrument: it would prohibit covered platforms from providing hosting or back-end services like content delivery and cyberattack protection to any outside entity, cutting off services that millions of small websites, businesses, and organizations depend on and forcing them to find new providers on a one-year clock.

The thresholds — $1.5 billion in global revenue and 30 million U.S. users — would sweep in far more companies than the handful of household-name platforms, and the one-year divestiture deadline leaves almost no room for orderly restructuring.

The $1,000,000-per-violation private right of action invites a wave of litigation whose merits a court system would have to sort out, since the bill provides no framework for defining a 'violation' at the level of an individual act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill took aim at a real and widely felt problem: dominant platforms competing against the businesses that sell through them. Its core self-preferencing and divestiture rules follow the same logic as historic antitrust separations. But the design is crude, and an honest supporter would have to acknowledge it: the blanket ban on providing hosting and internet infrastructure to outsiders would disrupt the web services ordinary businesses rely on every day, and the one-year, one-size-fits-all deadline is far more abrupt than comparable antitrust remedies. A narrower bill targeting self-preferencing alone would likely have attracted broader support. As written, the potential gains for competition came bundled with substantial risks of collateral damage. [S2][S3]

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Hawley introduced the bill on April 19, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor during the entire two-year Congress.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral — the bill simply sat in committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large tech platforms the bill targeted. Because the bill never advanced, Amazon, Google, and similar companies kept their combined marketplaces, self-preferencing practices, and cloud and hosting businesses exactly as they were; small sellers and consumers saw no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large tech platforms and their owners

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its name; recruited no cosponsors of either party before the Congress ended.

against.name: Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill during the two years it sat referred to the committee.

against.name: Major tech platforms (Amazon, Google, Microsoft)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against structural-separation and antitrust bills aimed at large platforms throughout the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever happened, so there is no roll call to divide on; the bill's fate was set at introduction, when a Republican senator sponsored it alone and not one of the 99 other senators, of either party, signed on.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms (Amazon, Google, and similar companies)
industries.note: The bill's whole point was to break up their integrated structure: no self-promotion on their own platforms, mandatory divestiture of affiliated sellers within a year, and a ban on acquisitions of sellers. Their revenue and market power depend on the practices the bill bans, so their interest ran directly against the bill's stated public purpose.

industries.industry: Cloud hosting and internet infrastructure (AWS, CDNs, security services)
industries.note: The bill would have prohibited covered platforms from providing hosting or back-end infrastructure — content delivery, DDoS protection, domain resolution — to any outside entity, and forced divestiture of those units within a year. Millions of small websites and businesses that depend on these services would have had to find new providers, so the industry's loss would have been ordinary customers' loss too.
